scope: Fresh independent offline review of the entire bound English prose and saved flow against the bound raw source and Chinese comparison; figures reviewed for textual context applicability only.
targetReader: Strong eight-year-old independent English self-reader, not a bilingual adult checking translation accuracy.

source.summary: All 12 original objects are represented in order: eight paragraph objects, two figures, and two captions. Source texts, references, kinds, IDs, and the embedded raw source are preserved. The English retains the Chinese edition's conditional corrections rather than restoring the raw textbook's universal claims.
details: The source's steel 1% example, rubber tens-of-percent example, lead below -100 degrees C example, and cast iron/steel printed stress and elongation values remain attributed textbook examples.

The English preserves the Chinese distinction between elastic recoverability and proportional Hooke-law behavior; it does not generalize large-strain rubber elasticity into universal linear elasticity.
The unreconciled-dataset warning, prohibition on combination with the previous Young's modulus example, approximate endpoint warning, and specimen-dependent ranges remain present.
Figure 89 and Figure 90 caption text is translated; unchanged figure identifiers and source labels remain provenance rather than a new visual approval.

science.summary: The essential scientific safeguards are preserved, but the brittleness paragraph leaves the small-total-deformation claim insufficiently scoped and gives a shared tensile definition to plasticity and ductility. Fix these local referents and definitions without removing the conditions or dataset warnings.
preservedSafeguards: Small deformation does not guarantee complete recovery in every material; material state, temperature, load, stress, damage, irreversible processes, and observation time matter.
Elasticity is recoverability, not necessarily linear stress-strain behavior. Plastic deformation is a permanent size or shape change after unloading.
Plastic and elastic labels are conditional responses, not fixed classifications of all steels, lead, or everyday plastics.
Temperature, composition, processing, loading rate, loading duration, and test conditions are distinguished rather than replaced by one universal threshold.
The -100 degrees C lead example is not a precise universal transition temperature or a guarantee of elastic response under every load.
Brittleness concerns little plastic deformation before fracture, not a universal stress-strain slope or the absolute absence of every plastic process.
Engineering stress uses original cross-sectional area; engineering strain uses original gauge length. The prose distinguishes local true stress using current local area after necking.
Ultimate tensile strength is defined as maximum engineering stress in tension, not silently equated with local true fracture stress.
The printed stress/strain dataset is UNRECONCILED and NOT verified material constants. It cannot support numerical material-parameter inference or combination with the earlier modulus example.
The 1%, 0.45%, and approximately 15% steel examples are not combined into a universal elastic or fracture threshold.

figureContextApplicability.summary: The English continues to associate Figure 89 with the textbook's cast iron specimen and Figure 90 with its steel specimen. It limits their use to the historical qualitative brittle/ductile comparison and retains the warning against precise endpoint readings or verified numerical inference.

figures.context: Cast iron specimen; little pronounced plastic elongation before fracture.
Steel specimen; comparison with fracture after substantial plastic elongation.

figureContextApplicability.limitation: No claim about actual axes, labels, pixels, endpoint placement, rendering, source-image fidelity, or the inventory's asset-hash claims is independently verified here. Readability findings on the surrounding English do not constitute a pixel finding.

readability.summary: Bilingual fidelity does not make this an independent eight-year-old reading text. Useful definitions have been added, but the opening introduces concepts after using them, proportionality remains unexplained, several everyday/technical meanings collide, industrial and graph vocabulary needs concrete first-use glosses, and the critical data warning remains adult analytical language.
positiveEvidence: Load, deformation, elasticity, permanent plastic deformation, relative elongation, original gauge length, and ultimate tensile strength have explicit English explanations.
The glass/porcelain examples provide a recognizable connection to breaking rather than only abstract material categories.
The industrial-process limitation and non-universal temperature and material warnings are retained.
Blank-line separation improves scanning, but does not by itself unpack the remaining abstract concepts.
readability.assessmentMethod: Direct reading of all eight English paragraph objects, both caption texts, and all 21 saved paragraphs, including first-use order and antecedents. No readability-score proxy or simulated child-test claim.

flow.summary: Saved-flow integrity passes: all 21 paragraph texts and their block mappings match the draft; boundaries at 7, 11, and 13 match the saved text pairs. Pedagogical flow still needs local revisions so definitions precede difficult uses and the unresolved-data caution is understood before the numerical examples.
flow.conceptSequence: Recoverable/permanent deformation; condition-dependent processing and temperature; brittleness; historical tensile comparison.
flow.recommendation: Keep the source-object order and conceptual boundaries. Improve sentences within the affected text blocks and update only their changed saved paragraphs and boundary text bindings; do not add a new lesson or reinterpret the printed numbers.

findings.title: Scope the small-total-deformation statement to brittle specimens
findings.evidence: In this section's tensile examples, the specimens fracture when their total deformation is still small.
findings.problem: The unqualified plural 'the specimens' can include both specimens subsequently named in the tensile comparison. The same lesson retains the steel specimen's approximately 15% fracture elongation. The intended brittle-material claim needs an explicit antecedent; a child should not have to infer that steel is excluded.
findings.recommendation: Change this sentence to explicitly describe the brittle specimen, for example: 'In the cast iron example in this section, the test piece breaks after only a small total stretch.' Keep the general definition based on very little plastic deformation; do not turn small total strain into the universal definition of brittleness.
findings.preserve: Specimen-specific steel behavior, approximately 15% source value, and the distinction between total deformation and permanent plastic deformation.

findings.title: Separate general plasticity from tensile ductility
findings.evidence: greater plasticity or ductility, meaning the ability to undergo appreciable plastic elongation in tension before breaking
findings.problem: The shared 'meaning' grammatically defines both plasticity and ductility as permanent elongation in tension. Plasticity is the broader permanent-deformation response already taught; ductility is the tensile ability being described here. 'Fracture', 'specimens', and 'tensile' also appear before concrete meanings are provided.
findings.recommendation: Use separate short definitions: plasticity means a lasting change in shape after the force is removed; ductility means the ability to stretch permanently before breaking. At first use, say fracture means breaking, a specimen is a test piece, and tension/tensile loading means pulling to stretch. Retain the condition-dependent comparison with steel, copper, and lead.
findings.preserve: Plasticity includes shape changes other than tensile elongation; ductility does not imply immunity to brittle fracture at every temperature, processing state, or load.

findings.title: Put the core meanings before the opening condition stack
findings.evidence: provided that the temperature and loading conditions are suitable, the deformation is sufficiently small, and no damage or significant irreversible process has occurred
findings.problem: The opening requires the reader to process deformation, loading conditions, and irreversible processes before the following sentences define even load and deformation. 'Material's state' and 'observation time' remain abstract. The first concept is obscured by qualifications that are important but not yet understandable.
findings.recommendation: Move the existing load/deformation meanings to the start and explain elasticity immediately as coming back toward the old size and shape after removing the force. Split the qualifications into short sentences; gloss irreversible as a change that does not undo itself, material state as its condition/preparation, and observation time as how long recovery is watched. Keep every substantive condition and 'many/approximately', not 'all/always'.
findings.preserve: Temperature, loading conditions, small deformation, damage, irreversible change, stress, material state, and time dependence; no guarantee of complete recovery.

findings.title: Explain proportional and percentage before contrasting linear and nonlinear elasticity
findings.evidence: Hooke's law states that stress is proportional to strain in the linear elastic range.
findings.problem: The sentence replaces an unfamiliar law with 'proportional' and 'linear elastic range' without explaining the relation. The next paragraph's nonlinear-elasticity distinction relies on that missing meaning. 'Relative elongation' has a ratio definition, but the reader receives no concrete interpretation of 1% or of the epsilon symbol's role.
findings.recommendation: Add a short explanation that strain is the fraction of the original length added by stretching, with 1% meaning one part in every hundred original parts, and that epsilon names this strain. Explain proportional as twice the stress giving twice the strain within that straight-line elastic range. Then state plainly that rubber may come back without following that doubling rule. Keep the source numbers as attributed examples, not general limits.
findings.preserve: The steel 1% example is not a universal limit; recoverability and proportionality are different; rubber's large recoverable strain does not generally establish Hooke's law.

findings.title: Disambiguate plastic behavior from the everyday material name
findings.evidence: wet clay, plastics, and lead ... so the textbook calls them "plastic materials."
findings.problem: A long first sentence introduces everyday plastics and technical 'plastic materials' together. 'Not a fixed classification' does not explicitly resolve their different meanings for a child. The following condition list uses composition, loading rate, load duration, and time-dependent response without concrete glosses.
findings.recommendation: Split the first sentence and explicitly say that plastic deformation means a lasting shape change, not simply being made of everyday plastic. Explain the condition list as what the material is made of, how quickly the force is applied, and how long it stays applied; describe time-dependent response as change that depends on how long the load acts or recovery is observed.
findings.preserve: Wet clay, plastics, and lead remain conditional textbook examples, not a fixed list of materials that always behave plastically.

findings.title: Name the industrial actions concretely when first used
findings.evidence: Under suitable hot-working conditions, steel or iron is usually easier to forge into shape than when cold.
findings.problem: Hot-working is unexplained and forge appears in saved paragraph 9 before forging is explained in paragraph 10. The preceding press example also assumes the child recognizes a machine rather than the everyday verb. The later definition 'shapes metal by applied forces' is still abstract.
findings.recommendation: At the first relevant use, say a press is a machine that squeezes metal, hot working means shaping hot metal, and forging means shaping metal by hammering or pressing. Keep this as a description of industrial work, not instructions. Preserve the limits on hot deformation and the lead temperature example's non-universal status.
findings.preserve: No do-it-yourself forging or lead-cooling activity; no unrestricted hot deformation or universal -100 degrees C transition.

findings.title: Make the two original reference measurements concrete
findings.evidence: engineering stress and engineering strain, which refer to the original cross-sectional area and original gauge length, respectively
findings.problem: The formulas are scientifically distinguished, but the reader has to understand cross-sectional area and track two quantities through 'respectively' before reaching their definitions. 'That original area' repeats an unexplained geometric term. N/m squared later appears without a plain unit meaning. This is a barrier to understanding what the two compared numbers actually measure.
findings.recommendation: Introduce each quantity separately before the compact pair: original cross-sectional area is the area straight across the test piece before stretching; original gauge length is the starting distance between the points used to measure its stretch. Explain stress as pulling force divided by that original area, and strain as added length divided by that original distance. Gloss N/m squared as newtons of force per square metre of area. Keep the current-local-area distinction for true stress and the explanation of necking.
findings.preserve: Engineering stress uses original area, not original length; engineering strain uses original length, not area. Do not replace either with necked current dimensions or imply the printed numbers have been verified.

findings.title: State the unresolved-data warning plainly before the printed numbers
findings.evidence: the original numerical dataset and curves have not been quantitatively reconciled or verified as material constants
findings.problem: This essential warning follows two numerical assertions and uses quantitatively reconciled, qualitative, numerical inferences, and verified material parameters. A self-reading child may treat the numbers as established facts without understanding the limitation. Later warnings are present, but their adult terminology does not repair the first interpretation.
findings.recommendation: Before the first numerical pair, add or move a short plain-language warning that the textbook's printed numbers and curves are still unresolved and are not verified material constants. Say they are retained only to compare the kinds of behavior, not to calculate reliable material properties. Keep the explicit ban on combining them with the earlier Young's modulus example, the approximate cast iron endpoint warning, and the specimen-specific/non-universal steel ranges; simplify those sentences without weakening them.
findings.preserve: UNRECONCILED, NOT verified material constants; no substituted modern values, new numerical reconciliation, universal threshold inference, or verified stiffness/strength calculation.

findings.title: Explain steepness and stiffness without redefining brittleness
findings.evidence: how rapidly stress rises with elongation depends on their stiffness and test conditions
findings.problem: The final comparison depends on stiffness and curve steepness. Earlier text only labels Young's modulus as describing stiffness; it does not explain stiffness or the graph relation in concrete terms. A child can miss why curve steepness is not the criterion for brittle behavior.
findings.recommendation: Give one short explanation tied to the defined quantities: in the same kind of tensile comparison, a steeper stress-versus-strain curve means a larger stress increase for the same small increase in strain. Then restate that brittle behavior concerns little permanent deformation before breaking, not all brittle materials sharing one slope. Retain the test-condition and 'almost no', rather than absolutely none, qualifications.
findings.preserve: No universal brittle-material stiffness or slope; no numerical slope calculation from this unresolved dataset; no claim that brittle materials have zero plastic processes in every condition.
